newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CZECH MATES SET TO CLASH AT OLD TRAFFORD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CZECH MATES SET TO CLASH AT OLD TRAFFORD.

text.p: The last time Patrik Berger and Karel Poborsky appeared together at Old Trafford they played as team mates who embraced in triumph as the Czech Republic beat France on penalties in the Euro 96 semifinals in June.
On Saturday they return as opponents as Poborsky's Manchester United try to become the first side this season to beat a Liverpool team who have unearthed a goalscoring gem in Berger.
The two Czechs were travelling back to England together on Thursday after playing in the republic's 0-0 draw with Spain in Wednesday's World Cup qualifier in Prague.
But although they are friends, the spirit of friendship will be suspended for at least 90 minutes on Saturday.
Not long ago it would have been unrealistic to imagine foreigners like Berger and Poborsky appearing in the biggest fixture in the English league.
But the barriers have fallen following the Bosman ruling on freedom of movement and other rule changes which have removed the restrictions on the number of overseas players per team.
In fact, as many as seven of the 22 players who start Saturday's match could be foreign -- although few can equal the impact Berger has made since his arrival in England.
Last month the 22-year-old striker, who lives just outside the city with his wife Jarka and son Patrik, scored five times for Liverpool in three matches in 11 days.
Critics began comparing him with Liverpool greats Ian Rush, Kenny Dalglish and Kevin Keegan after the two outstanding solo goals he netted in the 5-1 win over Chelsea on September 21.

The former Borussia Dortmund player has made such an impression that he kept 8.5 million pound signing Stan Collymore out of the starting lineup against Chelsea, although they may line up alongside each other against United if Robbie Fowler is unfit.
Liverpool manager Roy Evans says the Czech is even better than he originally believed.

"It was only after we watched him in the reserves that we realised he could play in more positions than we had thought. He can operate up front, off the front, or from the midfield. He is great at getting forward, is very aware of what is going on around him, has two very good feet and scores goals."
Berger had a successful run at Dortmund last season, winning a championship medal -- something he has in common with Poborsky, who helped Slavia Prague to their first Czech title for 47 years.
Poborsky, 24, could still be playing in Prague but for two outstanding performances in Euro 96m which alerted the talent scouts to his dazzling skills.

The first came when the Czechs beat Italy 2-1 at Anfield and Poborsky became one of the few players ever to get the better of Italian skipper Paolo Maldini, bewitching him with the ball control, aggression and speed which have earned him the nickname "The Express Train."
The second was his gravity-defying lob over Portuguese goalkeeper Vitor Baia which gave the Czechs a 1-0 quarterfinal win at Villa Park.
"It just happened, it was natural," Poborsky said. "It was a natural instinct, a choice I made in a split second, not planned at all."
It was that skill that tempted United manager Alex Ferguson to sign him for 3.5 million pounds in the close season.
Poborsky has not made quite the same impact at Old Trafford and, apart from one outstanding performance against Leeds, is still coming to terms with the speed of the English league.
Some say he runs into too many blind alleys and is greedy -- but he believes he is still learning and adapting his game. He has scored once in his eight appearances for United.
Like Berger, he is married with a young son, Patrik, and like Berger has a mane of hair that would be the envy of any heavy metal musician.
Just about the only thing Berger has been criticised for is using a girl's headband to keep his hair off his face -- which makes him look a little like Alice in Wonderland.

Poborsky's wild mane somehow seems plastered to his head when he plays but he has no intention of shaving it off, Eric Cantona-style. "It's been like this for three years," he says, "and I'm not ready to change it yet."
